name: Aaron Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I set three CNC lathes making hydraulic fittings for tractors and diggers. CNC means the machine follows a programmed cut; I load bar stock, set tools and measure the first fitting. I hold a vocational certificate and earn above the usual operator rate after eleven years, though a broken tool still spoils my afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Maya works as a nurse, and our school-age children Sofia and Daniel live with us under the same mortgage. We have about ten months saved, partly because I went through a factory closure before; other machine shops are nearby. I use an AI chat tool now and then to explain drawing notes, after checking the printed dimensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lads at the lathes that a useful drawing note beats a grand AI forecast. The hydraulic fitting still has to pass a micrometer check before it leaves my station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machines and my higher wage can carry on, and Maya’s nursing pay gives us another income. We have ten months saved because I remember how the bakery-equipment plant closed, not because I expect trouble every Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting my three lathes and checking the first part of each batch. I would keep using a chat tool now and then for drawing notes, as I already do, and put a fresh amount from full paid months into our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm in this picture. There is plenty of similar machine work nearby if this firm loses one contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the old plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer left, the orders thinned, and then the doors closed. That is why I like seeing ten months of bills in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new tool now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a new drawing feature only if it solved a real lathe problem. At the moment I use the same chat tool as before, so there is no new training planned.

say: I would tell the **lathe crew** a drawing note is useful without expecting miracles.
I would still measure the **first fitting** with a micrometer.
think: My **higher wage** and Maya’s nursing pay cover the household.
Ten **months saved** protect us after I lived through an earlier plant closure.
do: Keep **three lathes** running and check first parts.
Keep using the **existing chat tool** for drawing notes.
Add fresh **full-month wages** to our reserve.
feel: **Calm** about work with two incomes and nearby jobs.
S0.quote: I would test a new drawing feature only if it solved a real lathe problem.
fieldNote: His **previous closure** explains the reserve without making today’s factory insecure.
The current chat tool is an **existing habit**; new savings come from fresh paid wages.

steps.text: Keep setting three lathes and checking first fittings
Add fresh full-month wages to household reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the union should get a look at new machine plans before a camera appears on our floor. If the firm gains output, the people who set the tools deserve paid training and a share of the gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and programming could move to software before robots spread into hands-on loading. My tool-setting hours might shrink, even though there are other plants nearby and Maya’s nurse wage and our reserve give us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union rep for the planned staffing numbers and watch two colleagues try the new system. If the college offers a funded CAM programming place after my shift, and Maya can cover the children those evenings, I would enrol and learn to write toolpaths; I would also practise a new AI drawing checker on my own parts only after the firm provides paid training and a safe test copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own hours, but I can try a course without putting the mortgage on a card. I want to see a clean cut, not a sales slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a real seat is open, who pays the fee, and when the two evening classes finish. Maya’s hospital rota must cover Sofia and Daniel before I accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the drawing checker change a setting automatically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would compare its suggested dimensions with the print and measure a scrap part before any paid batch. A qualified setter should be beside me for the first trial.

say: I would demand **worker input** before camera tools change the floor.
I would ask for **paid training** alongside any new output target.
think: Software may reduce my **tool-setting hours** before physical robots spread.
Maya’s **nursing pay** and our reserve give me room to test a route.
do: Ask the **union rep** for staffing figures and observe two colleagues.
Enrol in **funded CAM training** only with an open seat, workable evenings and childcare.
Learn the **new AI checker** only after paid safe instruction on test parts.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with room to act.
S1.quote: I want to see a clean cut, not a sales slide.
fieldNote: His **steady approach** begins with colleagues’ real results before a course commitment.
CAM enrolment needs an **offered seat**; AI learning needs paid safe instruction on a test part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI could program lathes by 2028, while capable hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A quick software purchase could thin our setter hours before any robot lifts a bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect much of my setting pay to go early and most machine work to follow when robots can tend all three lathes. Maya’s wage and ten months saved help, but losing my higher wage would end our mortgage plan; I remember the last closure and would lie awake again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned summer trip, keep paid shifts while offered, and put new surplus wages into the reserve. If my hours are cut, I would apply for posted reachable machining or maintenance work only where the pay covers our bills, and ask the union to press for wage support before the last shift ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by that expected large wage loss. A reserve buys months, not another occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you abandon the CAM course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pause an unaccepted place because AGI could write those programs by 2028. If a paid course led to a posted maintenance job at adequate pay, I would assess it, but no such offer exists yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Maya work more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She could ask the hospital, but the rota and children’s care must fit. I would not count extra nursing wages before they appear on her payslip.

say: I would separate **2028 lathe programming** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I would ask the **union for wage support** before layoffs.
think: I expect **setting pay** to fall early and machine hours later.
Ten **months saved** cannot replace my higher wage indefinitely.
do: Cancel **summer trip** and keep paid shifts while available.
Save fresh **surplus wages** during full work months.
Apply after **actual cuts** only for posted reachable bill-covering machining or maintenance work.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless closure memories.
S2.quote: A reserve buys months, not another occupation.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking change** touches programming before 2031 robots can tend the lathes.
He pauses an **unaccepted course**; any later job application still needs a local posting and adequate pay.

steps.text: Cancel planned summer trip after fast AGI news

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI around 2031 and capable lathe robots around 2034 give us time to bargain for paid instruction. The union should ask which maintenance jobs will really be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still be paying the mortgage and helping Sofia and Daniel through school. A maintenance ticket might buy some paid years if an employer needs people to repair robot cells, but I cannot assume it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would review posted reachable maintenance vacancies and their wages this year. If the college offers a funded course with a real seat outside my paid shifts, Maya’s rota covers the children and a posted job pays our bills, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that job and keep my lathe shifts until an offer comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years gives me time to see whether the maintenance posts exist. I do not want to buy a certificate that ends up in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at postings first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last plant promised retraining after its big customer left, and the nearby jobs paid far less. I want a wage and travel time on paper before taking a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work on robot cells?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with an isolated machine and a qualified fitter teaching the first repair. I would learn those controls if the funded course actually provides that safe practical place.

say: I would ask for **real maintenance postings** before 2034 robots.
I would seek **paid safe instruction** through the union.
think: The **mortgage and school bills** remain at forty-eight.
A **maintenance ticket** has value only with adequate local work.
do: Review **posted local vacancies** and wages now.
Enrol in **funded maintenance training** only with a seat, childcare and adequate job.
Apply after **qualification** for the posted bill-covering role while keeping lathe shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to verify a real route.
S3.quote: I do not want to buy a certificate that ends up in a drawer.
fieldNote: His **past closure** makes him check wages and travel before paying time to training.
The proposed **practical robot learning** depends on an offered funded safe place; later employment needs a posted role and offer.

steps.text: Review posted reachable maintenance vacancies and wages this year
Enrol if funded maintenance seat fits childcare and adequate job exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable machine-tending robots around 2039 give us a decade to negotiate. We should set paid training terms while the lathes still need operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive, and fifty-six when capable robots might tend the bars. The mortgage should be smaller, but I cannot promise Maya’s rota, my health or a vacancy that far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep setting lathes and pay an extra amount from each full wage month toward mortgage principal. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual hours with posted local jobs; if shifts shrink, I would apply only for safe reachable work at a wage our household can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant change while our current wages stay secure. I want the kids to see us make choices from actual work, not a rumour about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get the pension figures and mortgage balance first. If those numbers cannot cover our bills, I will keep looking for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid course time and a written chance to apply for posted maintenance jobs. A vacancy list on the wall is more useful than a promise about everybody being fine.

I would separate **2036 thinking AI** from 2039 tending robots.
think: The **mortgage** may shrink, but future health and shifts are uncertain.
Current **two-wage security** lets us plan without pretending work is guaranteed.
do: Keep **2026 lathe shifts** and pay extra mortgage principal from new wages.
Ask the **union for written vacancies** and paid course terms.
Apply after **post-2036 cuts** only for posted reachable safe bill-covering work.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant machines while current wages remain sound.
S4.quote: I want the kids to see us make choices from actual work, not a rumour about 2039.
fieldNote: His **2026 shifts** are current; post-2036 job moves depend on continued employment and actual cut hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because programming could shrink early and robot tending could take most lathe hours by 2031. Written staffing dates, funded safe training and posted reachable jobs at adequate wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to inspect the robot before a shift is changed. The tool setter knows which scrap part tells the truth.

headlineQuote: The tool setter knows which scrap part tells the truth.
portrait: **Aaron**, 43, sets CNC lathes for hydraulic fittings with a vocational certificate and an above-typical operator wage.
His **nurse partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, ten-month reserve and plentiful nearby machine shops give him options.
He uses **AI occasionally** for drawing notes and adopts work tools after colleagues prove them on safe test parts.
Fast AGI threatens **lathe programming** before physical robots arrive; longer warning supports conditional maintenance training and mortgage repayment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut programming hours before capable tending robots threaten most lathe work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe training and posted nearby roles at bill-covering wages would help.
